objectives: Estimate how much choosing the best of many models inflates its score.

screens.title: The best of 40
screens.prose: A researcher tunes a trend rule over 40 lookbacks, from 5 to 200 days, on 3 years of daily data. The market is simulated with no trend at all. The best lookback, 200 days, shows a Sharpe ratio of 1.05.
screens.question: What Sharpe ratio should you expect from the 200-day rule over the next 3 years?

options.why: You took the winner's score as its skill. Every lookback is noise here; 1.05 is the luck of the best of 40.

options.text: About 0.5: some of it is luck
options.why: A haircut assumes part of the 1.05 is real. With no trend in the market, none of it is.
Overfitting does not make the future worse than noise here. A noise rule earns about 0 next time.

The 40 bars are 40 draws of noise. The tallest is just the luckiest.
Fresh data owe nothing to an old maximum. A noise rule's next Sharpe is about 0.

explain.text: You met this in the testing course: a maximum chosen in sample owes nothing to the future. Here it is the shape of every grid search. This lesson measures how big the luck of the best is, and what to do about it.

screens.title: How the best grows
screens.prose: Each noise strategy's Sharpe over $T = 3$ years is roughly normal with spread $1/\sqrt 3$. The blue line is the exact mean of the best of $N$; the dashed line is the rule of thumb $\sqrt{2 \ln N}/\sqrt 3$. Slide $N$.
screens.question: What is the smallest $N$ whose mean best reaches a Sharpe of 1.0?

widget.label: Smallest N
widget.accept: 15 exactly: 1.00. At 14 the mean best is 0.98.

feedback.correct: Fifteen noise strategies are enough, on average, for a best Sharpe of 1.0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Step $N$ up and read the mean best in the caption.

byKey.fourteen: At 14 the mean best is 0.98, just short. One more gets there.
byKey.thumb: You read the dashed rule of thumb, which runs high. Use the blue exact line.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def expected_max_sharpe(n_trials, n_obs, seed, sims):
    """Mean of the best annualised Sharpe among n_trials
    noise strategies, each with n_obs daily returns."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    se = np.sqrt(252 / n_obs)   # 1 / sqrt(years)
    sharpes = rng.standard_normal((sims, n_trials)) * se
    best = sharpes.max(axis=1)
    return round(float(best.mean()), 2)
widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests. Eight compare your rounded mean with math.isclose; the last checks that one strategy gives a mean best within 0.01 of 0. Each run draws at most 2 million normals. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Use `se = np.sqrt(252 / n_obs)` and take the maximum along each row.

byKey.test-1: Your best of 100 over 5 years is not 1.12. Check the spread: $1/\sqrt T$ with $T$ in years, so `np.sqrt(252 / n_obs)`.
byKey.test-9: One strategy should give a mean best of about 0: with $N = 1$ there is nothing to choose.

explain.text: The best of 100 noise strategies over 5 years averages 1.12, exactly as in the testing course; the exact value is $2.5076 / \sqrt 5 = 1.121$. With $N = 1$ it is about 0: one try has no maximum to inflate. The inflation comes from choosing, not from any single fit.

The **deflated Sharpe ratio** does this properly, allowing for skewed returns and correlated tries; the financial ML course treats it in its Lesson 11.

screens.title: Forty lookbacks, nearly one trial
screens.prose: Edge case. Lookbacks of 100 and 105 days trade almost the same positions, so their Sharpes move together. Here 40 noise strategies share a common part: each pair has correlation 0.9. Each run is one search over 3 years.

params.xLabel: Best Sharpe among 40 correlated noise strategies

screens.question: Independent tries gave a mean best of 1.25. Where does the mean best of these 40 sit?

options.why: You counted lookbacks, not independent chances. Correlated tries rise and fall together, so the best gains little.
Correlation 0.9 is not 1. The small independent part still gives a little to choose from.
Correlation narrows the spread between tries. Less spread means less to gain by picking the best.

hints.text: Run 1,000 searches and look where the bars pile up.
If every try moved together exactly, how many choices would there really be?
Only the independent part, with spread $\sqrt{0.1}$, can be chosen on: $\sqrt{0.1} \times 1.25 \approx 0.39$.

feedback.correct: Correlated tries inflate far less: about 0.39.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run the searches and see where the bars centre.

byKey.same: You counted lookbacks, not independent chances. Tries that move together offer little to choose between.

explain.text: Each try is a shared part plus an independent part with spread $\sqrt{0.1} = 0.32$, so the mean best is $0.32 \times 1.25 = 0.39$. With correlation 1, all 40 are one try and the inflation is 0. What counts is the **effective** number of trials, smaller than the raw count when tries move together.

screens.title: "We only tried three"
screens.prose: A researcher plots 30 candidate signals, drops the 27 that look flat, and backtests the other 3 properly. The best of the 3 has a Sharpe of 1.2 over 3 years. Her note says: we tried three.
screens.question: How many trials should the haircut count?

options.why: You counted only the backtests. Choosing 3 of 30 by looking at their charts already tested all 30 against the data.
Reporting one result does not undo the others. Every idea that met the data is a trial.
The 3 backtested signals were among the 30. Count each idea once.

hints.text: Which signals met the data before the backtests began?
Looking at a chart and dropping a signal is a decision made with the data.
All 30 were judged on the data. Count 30; with $N = 30$ the noise best is 1.18.

feedback.correct: Thirty ideas met the data, so $N = 30$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count every idea that was judged on the data, by eye or by backtest.

byKey.three: You counted only the backtests. The 27 dropped by eye were tested too, just informally.

explain.text: With $N = 3$ the noise best is 0.49 and 1.2 looks strong; with $N = 30$ it is 1.18 and 1.2 is ordinary. Choices made while looking at the data count as trials even when no model was fitted. This is the **garden of forking paths**.

screens.title: Count from the log
screens.prose: The fix is a **research log**: every idea that meets the data gets a line, including the ones that failed or were dropped by eye. Then $N$ is a count, not a memory.

widget.solution:
def trials_log_count(log):
    """log: (action, config) events in time order.
    A trial is a config that met the data: fitted ("fit")
    or judged by eye ("look"). "note" and "drop" add none.
    Returns the number of distinct trials."""
    return len({config for action, config in log
                if action in ("fit", "look")})

screens.title: The rule
screens.prose: For $N$ independent noise strategies over $T$ years, the best Sharpe averages a little under $$\frac{\sqrt{2 \ln N}}{\sqrt T}.$$ A reported best is believable only once you subtract this. The honest alternatives: a locked test set used once, nested CV, or a multiple-testing bar such as Bonferroni.
screens.question: By the rule, what Sharpe does the best of 40 noise strategies over 3 years reach?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $\sqrt{2 \ln 40}$, then divide by $\sqrt 3$.

byKey.exact: That is the exact simulated mean. The rule of thumb runs higher: compute $\sqrt{2\ln 40}/\sqrt 3$.
byKey.nosqrtT: You stopped at $\sqrt{2\ln 40}$. Divide by $\sqrt 3$ to turn it into a 3-year Sharpe.

explain.text: $\sqrt{2 \ln 40} = 2.716$ and $2.716/\sqrt 3 = 1.57$, above the exact 1.25. The rule is a cautious ceiling; the simulation is the better estimate.

screens.title: Where the rule comes from
screens.prose: Two facts from the testing course: a noise Sharpe over $T$ years is about $Z_i / \sqrt T$ with $Z_i$ standard normal, and the largest of $N$ standard normals seldom passes $\sqrt{2 \ln N}$. Chain them into the rule.
screens.question: Put the lines of the argument in order.

lines.text: $\widehat{\mathrm{SR}}_i \approx Z_i / \sqrt T$ for each of the $N$ noise strategies
$\max_i \widehat{\mathrm{SR}}_i \approx (\max_i Z_i) / \sqrt T$, since dividing by the same $\sqrt T$ keeps the order
$\max_i Z_i \lesssim \sqrt{2 \ln N}$, the bound for $N$ standard normals
$\max_i \widehat{\mathrm{SR}}_i \lesssim \sqrt{2 \ln N} / \sqrt T$, combining the last two lines

hints.text: Start from one strategy's Sharpe.
Move the maximum through the division by $\sqrt T$, and bound the maximum of the $Z_i$.
One Sharpe, then the maximum of them, then the bound on $\max Z_i$, then the two combined.

feedback.correct: One Sharpe, its maximum, the bound, the rule.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Begin with a single noise Sharpe and end with the rule.

byKey.d: The rule combines the two lines before it, so it comes last.
byKey.a: Everything rests on what one noise Sharpe looks like, so that line comes first.

explain.text: Dividing every $Z_i$ by the same $\sqrt T$ keeps their order, so the maximum divides too. The bound on $\max_i Z_i$ then gives $\sqrt{2\ln N}/\sqrt T$. More tries raise the bar slowly; more years lower it.

screens.question: What Sharpe would the desk believe, after the haircut?

hints.text: Subtract what noise gives the best of 40 over 3 years.
The simulated noise best is 1.25.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the simulated noise best, 1.25, from 1.30.

byKey.raw: That is the reported best. Take off what the best of 40 noise strategies gives.
byKey.thumb: You used the rule of thumb, a ceiling. The simulated 1.25 is the better estimate; either way little is left.

ideas: The best of $N$ noise strategies grows like $\sqrt{2\ln N}/\sqrt T$: 1.12 for 100 tries over 5 years, 1.25 for 40 over 3.
Haircut a reported best by what noise gives its $N$; correlated tries count as fewer, one pre-set try as none.
Every idea that met the data is a trial, fitted or not: keep a research log, and score the winner once on a locked test set.

quiz.question: How much selection inflation is in the 0.7?

options.text: None: with one try there is no best to choose

options.why: You applied a haircut by habit. With $N = 1$ the noise best is 0, so nothing is taken off.

options.text: All of it, as with any backtest
options.why: Selection inflation comes from choosing among tries. One pre-set try has none, though it still has ordinary noise.
$\ln 1 = 0$, so the rule gives 0: no inflation.

feedback.correct: $N = 1$: nothing to choose, nothing to deflate.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how many tries the 0.7 was chosen from.

byKey.some: With one pre-set try the noise best is 0, so the haircut is 0.

quiz.prose: A walk-forward test gives five fold Sharpes: 0.2, −0.4, 1.6, 0.1 and −0.3. The note reports 1.6, "on the most recent regime". Fold 3 is not the most recent.
quiz.question: What is the honest summary: the mean fold Sharpe?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the five fold Sharpes and divide by 5.

byKey.best: 1.6 is the best fold. Reporting it is selection among 5 folds.

explain.text: The five folds sum to 1.2, so the mean is 0.24. Reporting the best fold is choosing the best of 5 tries.

quiz.prose: A team chose the best of 200 settings by cross-validation on 2010 to 2020.
quiz.question: Which gives an honest estimate of how the chosen setting will do?

options.text: Score it once on 2021 to 2024, held back from the search
Its CV score from the search
options.why: That score is the best of 200, so it carries selection inflation.

options.text: Re-test the top 10 on 2021 to 2024 and keep the best
options.why: Choosing among 10 on the test years turns them into a search too.

options.text: Rerun the search with more folds
options.why: More folds sharpen each score, but the best of 200 is still inflated.

feedback.correct: A locked test set used once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the option where the score was not used to choose.

byKey.retest: Keeping the best of 10 on the test years is a new search.

explain.text: A test set used once, after the choice, has no selection in it. Nested CV does the same job inside the data; Bonferroni raises the bar instead.
